To this they add another sin, that they complain of being unjustly oppressed by God.<div eID="gen4128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4129" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But the God of your father</hi>. Why does he not also acknowledge God as his own God, unless because Satan had so fascinated his mind already, that he chose rather to wander in darkness than to turn to the light presented before him? Willingly or unwillingly, he is compelled to yield to the God of Abraham; and yet he defrauds him of the glory which is due, by retaining those fictitious deities by which he had been deceived. We see then that the ungodly, even when they have had proof of the power of God, yet do not entirely submit themselves to his authority. Wherefore, when God manifests himself to us, we must also seek from heaven the spirit of meekness, which shall bend and subdue us to obedience unto himself.<div eID="gen4129" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4127" osisID="Gen.31.29" type="section"/>
entries.5c06fd22586be7858f30029ceffaf8e5cb88d559: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.30" sID="gen4130" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4131" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30. </hi><hi type="italic">Wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?</hi> <note n="96"> <div sID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> “Wonderful is the madness of idolatry. He confesses that those whom he calls his gods, might yet be carried off by theft. It was the part of impiety that he worshipped idols; but it was the part of the folly that he declared those to be gods, who were unable to preserve themselves from being stolen.” — <hi type="italic">Rivetus</hi> in Gen., p. 656.<div eID="gen4132" type="x-p"/> </note> The second head of accusation which is alleged against Jacob is, that he had not departed through love to his country, nor for any just and probable cause; but that, in fact, he was implicated in an act of robbery. Heavy and disgraceful charge, of which Jacob was far from being guilty! But we learn hence, that no one can live so innocently in the world, but he must sometimes bear undeserved reproach and marks of infamy. Whenever this may happen to us, let that precious promise sustain us, that the Lord, in his own time, will bring forth our innocence as the morning light. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.37.6">Psalm 37:6</reference>.) For by this artifice Satan attempts to seduce us from the practice of well-doing, when, without any fault of ours, we are traduced by false calumnies. And since the world is ungrateful, it often makes the very worst return for acts of kindness. Some, indeed, are found, who, with heroic magnanimity, despise unfavourable reports, because they esteem the testimony of a good conscience more highly than depraved popular opinion. But it behoves the faithful to look to God, that their conscience may never fail them. We see that Laban calls his gods <foreign xml:lang="he"> תרפים</foreign>(<hi type="italic">teraphim</hi>,) not because he thought the Deity was enclosed within them; but because he worshipped these images in honor of the gods. Or rather, because, when he was about to pay homage to God, he turned himself to those images. At this day, by the sole difference of a word, the Papists think they skilfully effect their escape, because they do not attribute to idols the name of gods. But the subterfuge is frivolous, since in reality they are altogether alike; for they pour forth before pictures or statues whatever honor they acknowledge to be due to the one God. To the ancient idolaters the pretext was not wanting, that by a metonymy they styled those images gods, which were formed for the sake of representing God.<div eID="gen4131" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4130" osisID="Gen.31.30" type="section"/>
entries.a9d45834995930451d8f297f50470ed1ba54f37e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.31" sID="gen4133" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31. </hi><hi type="italic">And Jacob answered</hi>. He briefly refutes each head of the accusation: with respect to his secret departure, he modestly excuses himself, as having been afraid that he might be deprived of his wives. And in this way he takes part of the blame to himself, deeming it sufficient to exonerate himself from the malice of which he was thought to be guilty. He does not dispute, as a casuist, whether it was lawful to depart by stealth; but leaves it undetermined whether or not his fear was culpable. Let all the children of God learn to imitate this modesty, lest through an immoderate desire to vindicate their own reputation, they should rush into contentions: just as we have seen many raise tragic scenes out of nothing, because they will not endure that any censure, however trifling, should be cast upon them. Jacob, therefore, was content with this excuse, that he had done nothing wickedly. His defense on the other charge follows, in which Jacob shows his confidence, by adjudicating the person to death, with whom the things stolen should be found. <note n="97"> <div sID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> “Jacob might cover himself with the shield of his own innocence; but it was not large enough to cover all others, not even his most beloved wife, whom he, in ignorance, adjudicates to death, and incautiously gives sentence against her.” — <hi type="italic">Rivetus</hi> in Gen, p. 657.<div eID="gen4135" type="x-p"/> </note> He speaks, indeed, from his heart; but if the truth had then been discovered, he must, of necessity, have been ashamed of his rashness. Therefore, though he was not conscious of guilt, he yet singled through excessive haste, in not having diligently inquired before he pronounced concerning a doubtful matter. He ought to have called both his wives and his children, and to have inquired of each how the affair stood. He was, indeed, persuaded, that his family was so well conducted, that no suspicion of the theft had ever entered into his mind; but he ought not so to have relied upon his own discipline, as to be free from fear when a crime is alleged against his family. Wherefore, let us learn to suspend our judgment in matters of which we are ignorant, lest we should repent too late of our temerity. We may add, that hence it happened, that the pollution which he might have exterminated immediately, continued still longer in the family of Jacob.<div eID="gen4134" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4133" osisID="Gen.31.31" type="section"/>
entries.cb6a66e903bb541b8314c27f6311e866aeab682b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.32" sID="gen4136" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32. </hi><hi type="italic">That Rachel had stolen them</hi>. Moses relates the manner in which Rachel had concealed her theft; namely, by sitting on the idols, and pretending the custom of women as her excuse. It is a question, whether she did this through shame or pertinacity. It was disgraceful to be caught in the act of theft; she also dreaded the severe sentence of her husband. Yet to me it appears probable that fear did not so much influence her as the obstinate love of idolatry. For we know how greatly superstition infatuates the mind. Therefore, as if she had obtained an incomparable treasure, she thinks that she must attempt anything rather than allow herself to be deprived of it. Moreover, she chooses rather to incur the displeasure of her father and her husband, than to relinquish the object of her superstition. To her stratagem she also adds lying words, so that she deserves manifold censure.<div eID="gen4137" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4136" osisID="Gen.31.32" type="section"/>
entries.1ce9709b56d1424ce07c7506a51c57e4f0a0f5e3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.36" sID="gen4138" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36. </hi><hi type="italic">And Jacob was wroth, and chode with Laban</hi>. Jacob again acts amiss, in contending with Laban about a matter not sufficiently known, and in wrongfully fastening on him the charge of calumny. For although he supposed all his family to be free from blame, yet he was deceived by his own negligence. He acts, indeed, with moderation, because in expostulating with Laban he does not use reproaches; but in this he is not to be excused, that he undertakes the cause of his whole family, when they were not exempt from blame. If any one should make the objection to this statement, that Jacob was constrained by fear, because Laban had brought with him a great band of companions: the circumstances themselves show, that his mind was thus influenced by moderation rather than by fear. For he boldly resists, and shows no sign of fear; only he abstains from the insolence of evil speaking. He then adds that he had just cause of accusation against Laban; not because he wished to rise in a spirit of recrimination against his father-in-law; but because it was right that the kindred and associates of Laban should be made witnesses of all that had passed, in order that, by the protracted patient endurance of Jacob, his integrity might be the more manifest. Jacob also calls to mind, not only that he had been a faithful keeper of the flock, but also that his labor had been rendered prosperous by the blessing of God; he adds, besides, that he had been held accountable for all losses. In this he insinuates against Laban the charge of great injustice: for it was not the duty of Jacob voluntarily to inflame the avarice and rapacity of his father-in-law, by attempting to soothe him; but he yielded, by constraint, to his injuries. When he says that sleep departed from his eyes, he not only intimates that he passed sleepless nights, but that he had so contended against nature itself, as to defraud himself of necessary repose.<div eID="gen4139" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4138" osisID="Gen.31.36" type="section"/>
entries.66d7168956454dee610a72a62e73b6fd0cdbf318: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.42" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.42" sID="gen4140" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">42. </hi><hi type="italic">Except the God of my father</hi>. Jacob here ascribes it to the favor of God, that he was not about to return home entirely empty; whereby he not only aggravates the sin of Laban, but meets an objection which might seem at variance with his complaints. He therefore denies that he has been made rich by the kindness of his father-in-law; but testifies that he has been favourably regarded by the Lord: as if he had said, I owe it not to thee, that thou hast not further injured me; but God, who is propitious to me, has withstood thee. Now, since God is not the defender of unfaithfulness, nor is wont to help the wicked, the integrity of Jacob may be ascertained from the fact that God interposed as his vindicator. It is also to be observed, that by expressly distinguishing the God of Abraham from all fictitious gods, he declares that there is no other true God: by which he, at the same time, proves himself to be a truly pious worshipper. The expression “the fear of Isaac,” is to be taken passively for the God whom Isaac revered; just as, on account of the reverence due to him, he is called the “fear and the dread” of his people. <note n="98"> <div sID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.13">Isaiah 8:13</reference>. “Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.”<div eID="gen4142" type="x-p"/> </note> A similar expression occurs immediately after, in the same chapter. Now the pious, while they fear God, are by no means horror — struck at his presence, like the reprobates; but trembling at his judgment, they walk circumspectly before him.<div eID="gen4141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4143" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">God has seen my affliction, and the labor of my hands</hi>. This was spoken from a pious feeling that God would bring help to him when afflicted, if he should conduct himself with fidelity and honesty. Therefore, in order that the Lord may sustain us with his favor, let us learn to discharge our duty rightly; let us not flee from our proper work; and let us not refuse to purchase peace by submitting to many inconveniences. Further, if they from whom we have deserved well treat us severely and unjustly, let us bear our cross in hope and in silence, until the Lord shall succor us: for he will never forsake us, as the whole Scripture testifies. But Jacob distinctly presses his father-in-law with his own confession. For why had God rebuked him, unless because he was persecuting an innocent man in defiance of justice and equity; for as I have lately intimated, it is abhorrent to the nature of God to favor evil and unjust causes.<div eID="gen4143" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.42" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4140" osisID="Gen.31.42" type="section"/>
entries.02ed5d24ad7b2d747f2dcb820c8cb77ca48b4f6f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.43" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.43" sID="gen4144" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">43. </hi><hi type="italic">These daughters are my daughters</hi>. Laban begins now to speak in a manner very different from before: he sees that he has no farther ground of contention. Therefore, being convinced, he buries all strife, and glides into placid and amicable discourse. “Why,” he asks, “should I be hostile to thee, when all things between us are common? Shall I rage against my own bowels? For both thy wives and thy children are my own blood; wherefore I ought to be affected towards you, as if you all were part of myself.” <note n="99"> <div sID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="la">Acsi gererem omnium personam</foreign>. “As if I bore the person or character of all,” perhaps, “as your representative — the one who personates you.” Yet, in the translation, the sense is given which will, perhaps, on the whole, be most intelligible to the reader. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen4146" type="x-p"/> </note> He now answers like an honorable man. Whence, then, has this humanity so suddenly sprung up in the breast of him who lately had been hurried onward, without any respect to right or wrong, to ruin Jacob; unless it were, that he knew Jacob to have acted towards him with fidelity, and to have been at length compelled by necessity to adopt the design of departing by stealth? And this was an indication that he was not absolutely desperate: for we may find many persons of such abandoned impudence, that though overcome and silenced by arguments, they yet do not cease to rush headlong in insane rebellion. From this passage we infer, that although avarice and other sinful affections take away judgment and soundness of mind; there yet remains a knowledge of truth engraven on the souls of men, which being stirred up emits scintillations, to prevent the universal triumph of depravity. If any one before had said, What does thou, Laban? What brutality is this to rage against thine own bowels? the remonstrance would not have been heard, for he burned with headstrong fury. But now he voluntarily suggests this to himself, and proclaims what he would have been unwilling to hear from another. It appears, then, that the light of justice which now breaks forth, had been smothered in his mind. In short, it is self-love alone which blinds us; because we all judge aright where personal interests are not concerned. If, however, it should so happen that we are for a time in perplexity, we must still seek to obey the dictates of reason and justice. But if any one hardens himself in wickedness, the interior and hidden knowledge, of which I have spoken, will yet remain engraven in his mind, and will suffice for his condemnation.<div eID="gen4145" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.43" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4144" osisID="Gen.31.43" type="section"/>
entries.1893d99008e69d196377cce3e7ba1b79fe8c5a4d: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.44" sID="gen4147" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">44. </hi><hi type="italic">Let us make a covenant, I and thou</hi>. Laban here acts as men conscious of guilt are wont to do, when they wish to guard themselves against revenge: and this kind of trepidation and anxiety is the just reward of evil deeds. Besides, wicked men always judge of others from their own disposition: whence it happens that they have fears on all sides. Moses before relates a somewhat similar example, when Abimelech made a covenant with Isaac. Wherefore we must take the greater care, if we desire to possess tranquil minds, that we act sincerely and without injury towards our neighbors. Meanwhile Moses shows how placable Jacob was, and how easily he permitted himself to be conciliated. He had endured very many and grievous wrongs; but now, forgetting all, he freely stretches out the hand of kindness: and so far is he from being pertinacious in defending his own right, that he, in a manner, anticipates Laban himself, being the first to take a stone, and set it up for a pillar. And truly it becomes the children of God, not only with alacrity to embrace peace, but even ardently to search for it, as we are commanded in <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.34.14">Psalm 34:14</reference> <note n="100"> <div sID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> “Depart from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.”<div eID="gen4149" type="x-p"/> </note> As to the heap of stones, it was always the practice to use some ceremony which might confirm the compact on both sides; on this occasion a heap of stones is raised, in order that the memory of the covenant might be transmitted to posterity. That Jacob took part in this was a proof, as we have said, of a mind disposed to peace. He freely complained, indeed, when it was right to do so; but when the season of pacification arrived, he showed that he cherished no rancour. Moses, in relating afterwards that they did eat there, upon the heap, does not observe the order of the history. For, on both sides, the conditions of the covenant were agreed upon and declared, before the feast was celebrated: but this figure of speech (as we have before seen) was sufficiently in use.<div eID="gen4148" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4147" osisID="Gen.31.44" type="section"/>
entries.fc4e3c28dd9e4c712b5cd4da43a3fb73e112b93a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.47" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.47" sID="gen4150" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">47. </hi><hi type="italic">And Laban called it</hi>. Each, in his own language, gives a name, of the same signification, to the heap. Whence it appears, that Laban used the Syrian tongue, though born of the race of Heber. But it is not wonderful that he, dwelling among Syrians, should have accustomed himself to the language as well as to the manners of the Syrians. And a little before, he is twice called a Syrian; as if Moses would describe him as degenerate, and alienated from the Hebrews. But this seems by no means accordant with the previous history, where we read that the daughters of Laban gave Hebrew names to their sons. Yet the solution is not difficult; for since the affinity between these languages was great, the inflection of one word into another was easy: besides, if the wives of Jacob were tractable, it is not surprising that they should have learned his language. And beyond doubt, he would himself make a point of this matter: seeing he knew that his family was separated from the rest of the nations. Moses, in using the name of Galeed, does it proleptically; for since he was writing for his own times, he does not scruple to give it the generally received name. Moreover we hence infer, that ceremonies and rites ought to refer to that which those who use them mutually agree upon. Which rule also ought to be applied to the sacraments; because if the word by which God enters into covenant with us be taken away, useless and dead figures will alone remain.<div eID="gen4151" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.47" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4150" osisID="Gen.31.47" type="section"/>
entries.abab3d15e1488650cfee570c62e2a2a0d8775294: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.49" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.49" sID="gen4152" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">49. </hi><hi type="italic">The Lord watch between me and thee</hi>. Laban commits to the judgment of God, for vengeance, whatever offense either of them should be guilty of against the other in his absence; as if he would say, “Though the knowledge of the injury should not reach me, because I shall be far distant, yet the Lord, who is everywhere present, will behold it.” Which sentiment he more clearly expresses afterwards, when he says, “No one is with us; God will be witness between me and thee.” By which words he means, that God will be a severe avenger of every wickedness, though there should be no judge upon earth to decide the cause. And certainly if there were any religion flourishing within us, the presence of God would influence us far more than the observation of men. But it arises from the brutal stupidity of our flesh, that we reverence men only; as if we might mock God with impunity, when we are not convicted by the testimony of men. If, then, this common feeling of nature dictated to Laban, that the frauds which were hidden from men would come into judgment before God; we who enjoy the light of the gospel should indeed be ashamed to seek a covert for our fallacies. Hence also, we gather the legitimate use of an oath, which the Apostle declares in his epistle to the Hebrews; namely, that men, in order to put an end to their controversies, resort to the judgment of God.<div eID="gen4153" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.49" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4152" osisID="Gen.31.49" type="section"/>
entries.e9ac6a8cbc2c485e00a92ec9827ec93c585bd9e7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.50" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.50" sID="gen4154" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">50. </hi><hi type="italic">If thou shalt take other wives besides my daughters</hi>. Laban declares that it would be a species of perfidy, if Jacob should take to himself any other wives. But he had himself compelled Jacob to the act of polygamy: for whence was it that the holy man had more wives than one, except that Leah had been craftily substituted in the place of Rachel? But he now, from a pure sentiment of nature, condemns the fault, of which, blinded by avarice, he had wickedly been the author. And certainly, when the bond of marriage is broken, than which none among men is more sacred, the whole of human society sinks into decay. Wherefore, those fanatical men, who, at this day, delight to defend polygamy, have no need of any other judge than Laban.<div eID="gen4155" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.50" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4154" osisID="Gen.31.50" type="section"/>
entries.1b463cccc4bd52c170ef47c2ce9a495f26c30062: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.53" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.53" sID="gen4156" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">53. </hi><hi type="italic">The God of Abraham</hi>. It is indeed rightly and properly done, that Laban should adjure Jacob by the name of God. For this is the confirmation of covenants; to appeal to God on both sides, that he may not suffer perfidy to pass unpunished. But he sinfully blends idols with the true God, between whom there is nothing in common. Thus, truly, men involved in superstitions, are accustomed to confound promiscuously sacred things with profane, and the figments of men with the true God. He is compelled to give some honor to the God of Abraham, yet he lies plunged in his own idolatrous pollution; and, that his religion may not appear the worse, he gives it the color of antiquity. For in calling him the God of his father, he boasts that this God was handed down to him from his ancestors. Meanwhile Jacob does not swear superstitiously. For Moses expressly declares, that he sware only by “the fear of Isaac;” whence we learn that he did not assent to the preposterous form of oath dictated by his father-in-law; no too many do, who, in order to gain the favor of the wicked, pretend to be of the same religion with them. But when once the only God is made known to us, we wickedly suppress his truth, unless by its light all the clouds of error are dispersed.<div eID="gen4157" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.53" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4156" osisID="Gen.31.53" type="section"/>
entries.ee9162ca1a5030efa4d3c41068147521f3654000: <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.54" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Gen.31.54" sID="gen4158" type="section"/> <div sID="gen4159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">54. </hi><hi type="italic">And called his brethren to eat bread</hi>. In courteously receiving his kindred, by whom he had been ill-treated, as his guests, Jacob showed his kindness. Moses also intimates that it was by the special favor of God that, after the most dreadful storm which threatened the holy man with destruction, a placid serenity suddenly shone forth. To the same cause is to be assigned what immediately follows, that Laban departed in a friendly manner: for by this method the Lord openly manifested himself as the guardian of his servant, seeing that he wonderfully delivered him as a lost sheep out of the jaws of the wolf. And truly, not only was the fury of Laban appeased; but he put on paternal affection, as if he had been changed into a new man.<div eID="gen4159" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Gen.31.54" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen4158" osisID="Gen.31.54" type="section"/>
entries.fb7a2713989833bd099416459ffb270416055013:
55. And blessed them. The character of the person is here to be noticed, because Laban, who had lapsed from true piety, and was a man of unholy and wicked manners, yet retained the habit of giving his blessing. For we are hereby taught, that certain principles of divine knowledge remain in the hearts of the wicked, so that no excuse may be left to them on the ground of ignorance; for the custom of pronouncing a blessing arises hence, that men are certainly persuaded that God alone is the author of all good things. For although they may proudly arrogate what they please to themselves; yet when they return to their right mind, they are compelled, whether they will or no, to acknowledge that all good proceeds from God alone.
CHAPTER 32.
Genesis 32:1-32
1. And Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
1. Postea Iahacob abiit in viam suam, et occurrerunt ei Angeli Dei.
2. And when Jacob saw them, he said, This is God’s host: and he called the name of that place Mahanaim.
2. Et dixit Iahacob, quando vidit eos, Castra Dei sunt haec: et vocavit nomen loci illius Mahanaim.
3. And Jacob sent messengers before him to Esau his brother unto the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
3. Misit autem Iahacob nuntios ante se ad Esau fratrem suum ad terram Sehir in regionem Edom.
4. And he commanded them, saying, Thus shall ye speak unto my lord Esau; Thy servant Jacob saith thus, I have sojourned with Laban, and stayed there until now:
4. Et praecepit eis dicendo, Sic dicentis domino meo Esau, Sic dixit servus tuus Iahacob, Cum Laban havitavi et moratus sum huc usque.
5. And I have oxen, and asses, flocks, and menservants, and womenservants: and I have sent to tell my lord, that I may find grace in thy sight.
5. Et sunt mihi boves et asini, pecudes et servi, et ancillae, et misi ut nuntiarem domino meo, ut invenirem gratiam in oculis tuis.
6. And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying, We came to thy brother Esau, and also he cometh to meet thee, and four hundred men with him.
6. Reversi autem sunt nuntii ad Iahacob, dicendo, Venimus ad fratrem tuum, ad Essau, et etiam pergit in occursum tuum, et quadringenti viri cum eo.
7. Then Jacob was greatly afraid and distressed: and he divided the people that was with him, and the flocks, and herds, and the camels, into two bands;
7. Et timuit Iahacob valde, et angustiis affectus est; et divisit populum, qui erat secum, et pecudes, et boves, et camelos in duas turmas.
8. And said, If Esau come to the one company, and smite it, then the other company which is left shall escape.
8. Dixit enim, Si veniret Essau ad turmam unam, et percusserit eam, turma, quae remanserit, evadet.
9. And Jacob said, O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac, the LORD which saidst unto me, Return unto thy country, and to thy kindred, and I will deal well with thee:
9. Et dixit Iahacob, Deus patris mei Abraham, et Deus patris mei Ishac, Domine, qui dixisti ad me, Revertere ad terram tuam et cognationem tuam, et benefaciam tibi.
10. I am not worthy of the least of all the mercies, and of all the truth, which thou hast shewed unto thy servant; for with my staff I passed over this Jordan; and now I am become two bands.
10. Minor sum cunctis misericordiis, et omni veritate, quam fecisti cum servo tuo: quai in baculo meo transivi Iordanem hunc, et nunc factus sum in duas turmas.
11. Deliver me, I pray thee, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau: for I fear him, lest he will come and smite me, and the mother with the children.
11. Erue me nunc de manu fratris mei, de manu Esau: timeo enim eum, ne ferte veniat, et percutiat me, matremque cum filiis.
12. And thou saidst, I will surely do thee good, and make thy seed as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.
12. Et tu dixisti, Benefaciendo benefaciam tibi, et ponam semen tuum sicut arenam maris, quae non numeratur prae multitudine.
13. And he lodged there that same night; and took of that which came to his hand a present for Esau his brother;
13. Et pernoctavit ibi nocte ipsa, et accepit ex iis, quae occurrebant ad manum suam, manus mittendum ad Esau fratrem suum.
14. Two hundred she goats, and twenty he goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams,
14. Capras ducentas et hircos viginti, oves ducentas et arietes viginti:
15. Thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine, and ten bulls, twenty she asses, and ten foals.
15. Camelos lactantes, et pullos earum triginta: vaccas quadraginta, et juvencos decem: asinas viginti, et pullos decem.
16. And he delivered them into the hand of his servants, every drove by themselves; and said unto his servants, Pass over before me, and put a space betwixt drove and drove.
16. Et dedit in manum servorum suorum, singulos greges seorsum: dixitque ad servos suos, Transite ante me, et interstitium ponetis inter gregem et gregem.
17. And he commanded the foremost, saying, When Esau my brother meeteth thee, and asketh thee, saying, Whose art thou? and whither goest thou? and whose are these before thee?
17. Et praecepit primo, dicendo, Si occurrerrit tibi Esau frater meus, et interrogaverit to, dicendo, Cujus es, et quo pergis, et cujus sunt ista ante to?
18. Then thou shalt say, They be thy servant Jacob’s; it is a present sent unto my lord Esau: and, behold, also he is behind us.
18. Dices, Servi tui Iahacob munus est, missum ad dominum meum Esau: et ecce etiam ipse est post nos.
19. And so commanded he the second, and the third, and all that followed the droves, saying, On this manner shall ye speak unto Esau, when ye find him.
19. Praecepit etiam secundo, etiam tertio, etiam cunctis pergentibus post greges, dicendo, Secundum verbum hoc loquemini ad Esau, quando invenietis eum.
20. And say ye moreover, Behold, thy servant Jacob is behind us. For he said, I will appease him with the present that goeth before me, and afterward I will see his face; peradventure he will accept of me.
20. Et dicetis etiam, Ecce servus tuus Iahacob est post nos: dixit enim, Placabo faciem ejus munere, quod vadit ante me, et postea videbo faciem ejus, si forte suscipiat faciem meam.
21. So went the present over before him: and himself lodged that night in the company.
21. Transivit itaque munus ante eum: et ipse pernoctavit nocte ipsa cum turma.
22. And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok.
22. Et surrexit nocte ipsa, et accepit duas uxores suas, et duas ancillas suas, et undecim liberos suos, et transivit vadum Jaboc.
23. And he took them, and sent them over the brook, and sent over that he had.
23. Et accepit eos, et transire fecit eos torrentem, transire, inquam, fecit omnia quae erant sibi.
24. And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.
24. Porro remansit Iahacob solus ipse: et luctatus est vir cum eo, donec ascendit aurora.
25. And when he saw that he prevailed not against him, he touched the hollow of his thigh; and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was out of joint, as he wrestled with him.
25. Et vidit quod non praevaleret ei, et tetigit palam femoris ejus, et movit se pala femoris Iahacob, luctante illo cum eo.
26. And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
26. Tunc dixit, Dimitte me, quia ascendit aurora. Cui respondit, Non dimittam to, nisi benedixeris mihi.
27. And he said unto him, What is thy name? And he said, Jacob.
27. Et dixit ad eum, Quod est nomen tuum? Et ait, Iahacob.
28. And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.
28. Tunc dixit, Non Iahacob dicetur ultra nomen tuum, sed Israel: quia princeps fuisti cum Deo, et hominibus praevalebis.
29. And Jacob asked him, and said, Tell me, I pray thee, thy name. And he said, Wherefore is it that thou dost ask after my name? And he blessed him there.
29. Et interrogavit Iahacob, et dixit, Indica, quaeso, nomen tuum. Et dixit, Utquid interrogas de nomine meo? et benedixit ei illic.
30. And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.
30. Vocavit ergo Iahacob nomen loci, Peniel: quia vidi Deum facie ad faciem, et evasit anima mea.
31. And as he passed over Penuel the sun rose upon him, and he halted upon his thigh.
31. Et ortus est ei sol, quando transivit Penuel, et claudicabat in femore suo.
32. Therefore the children of Israel eat not of the sinew which shrank, which is upon the hollow of the thigh, unto this day: because he touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh in the sinew that shrank.
32. Idciro non comedunt filii Israel nervum contractionis, qui est in pala femoris, usque ad diem hanc: quia tetigit palam femoris Iahacob in nervo contractionis.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="31" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 AND he heard the words of Labans sons, saying, Jacob hath taken away all that was our fathers: and of that which was of our fathers, hath he gotten all this glory <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These riches, which are called <ns0:hi>glory, Gen.</ns0:hi> 45. 13. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 49. 16. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 66. 12. compared with <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 60. 6. because their possessours use to glory in them, and by them gain glory and esteem from others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and behold, it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> not towards him <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> as yester<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />day and the day before.</ns0:note> as before <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And this change of his countenance argued a change in his mind and presaged some evil intentions in him towards <ns0:hi>Iacob.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And the LORD said unto Jacob, Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred, and I will be with thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> is first named here, as also <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 4. 11. because she was his chief, and, by right, his first and onely designed wife. And therefore it is observable, that in the enumeration of <ns0:hi>Ia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cobs</ns0:hi> Wives and Children, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 46. <ns0:hi>Leah</ns0:hi> is onely mentioned by her name, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. but <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>Iacobs wife, ver.</ns0:hi> 19. by way of eminency and in a peculiar manner.</ns0:note> to the field <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Where they might more freely discourse of their business and without fear or interruption.</ns0:note> unto his flocks.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And said unto them, I see your fathers coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tenance, that it is not toward me as before: but the God of my father hath been with me <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Either 1. Hath blessed me, hath stood constantly by me, when your father hath failed and deceived me. O<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, 2. Hath appeared unto me, as <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And ye know that with all my power <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Both of my mind and body, as I would have done for my self, as became a faithful servant to do.</ns0:note> I have served your father.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And your father hath deceived me, and chang<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed my wages <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Neh. 4. 12.</ns0:note> ten times <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Oft-times, as that certain number is commonly used, as <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26. 26. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 14. 22. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 19. 3. &c.</ns0:note>: but God suffered him not to hurt me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages, then all the cattle <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>All</ns0:hi> is here, as oft elsewhere, put for the greater or the bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter part, as appears from <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 31. 1, 8. Or, for all that <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> desired to be such.</ns0:note> bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ring-straked shall be thy hire <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Hence it appears that <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> through envy and covetousness did break his agreement made with <ns0:hi>Ia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cob</ns0:hi> and altered it as he thought meet, and that <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> patiently yielded to all such changes.</ns0:note>, then bare all the cattle ring-straked.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:31" />9 Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> to me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and behold, the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> he-goats.</ns0:note> rams which leaped upon the cattle, <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> ring-straked, speck<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led, and grizled <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which were marked with spots like hail in colour and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portion, as the word signifieth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And the Angel of God spake unto me in a dream, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Jacob; and I said, Here am I.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And he said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ring-straked, speckled, and grizled: for I have seen all that Laban doth unto thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 I am the God of Bethel, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 28. 18.</ns0:note> where thou anointedst the pillar, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> where thou vowedst a vow unto me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Of which see <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 28. 19, 20. And this God here men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions to shew his acceptance of that action of <ns0:hi>Iacobs,</ns0:hi> his mind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness even of the past and forgotten services of his people, and his purpose now to fulfil the promise there made to him.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> now <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 32. 9.</ns0:note> arise, get thee out from this land, and return unto the land of thy kindred.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And Rachel and Leah answered and said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him, Is there yet any portion or inheritance for us in our fathers house <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">We can expect no further benefit from him, but deceit and oppression, and injury, and therefore are willing to leave him.                   <ns0:p n="15">15 Are we not counted of him strangers <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">As if we had no more right to his estate than strangers.</ns0:note>? for he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 29. 15, 27.</ns0:note> hath sold us <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">In stead of a good part of his Estate which by the Law of God and Nature belongs to us, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 12. 14. wherewith he should have endowed us upon our Marriage, he hath made sale of us for this 14 years hard service, seeking onely his own, not our advantage.</ns0:note>, and hath quite devoured also our money <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Hath not onely with-held from us, but spent upon himself, that money which he got by thy care and indu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stry, whereof a considerable part was due in equity to us and to our Children.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 For all the riches which God hath taken from our Father, that is ours <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not onely by Gods special gift, but by the natural right which Children have to a share in his Estate, and upon the account of thy faithful and laborious service.</ns0:note> and our childrens: Now then whatsoever God hath said unto thee, do.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Then Jacob rose up, and set his sons, and his wives upon camels.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And he carried away all his cattle, and all his goods which he had gotten, the cattle of his getting, which he had gotten in Padan-aram, for to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And Laban went to shear his sheep: and Rachel had stollen the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Teraphim.</ns0:note> images that were her fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Quest. 1. What were those <ns0:hi>Teraphims</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>images? Ans.</ns0:hi> They were images made in the shape of men, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 13, 16. which the Gentiles worshipped as subordinate Gods, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 30, 32. of this chapter, to which they committed the protection of their Families, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>. which they used to consult a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout-secret or future things, and from which they received an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swers about them, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 21. 21. <ns0:hi>Zech.</ns0:hi> 10. 2. Of these see more <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 17. 5. and 18. 14, 17. &c. <ns0:hi>Ho<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

Why did <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> steal them? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Partly lest her father by consulting them should discover their flight and the course which they took; and partly because she seemed yet to retain a superstitious con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceit of them, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 2. Others, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they were pretty and precious things, made of Silver and Gold, which she took as a part of what was due to her both as his daughter and for her Husbands service. Others, that she might remove so great an occasion of her Fathers Idolatry, and shew him the vanity of such Gods as might be stoln away.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And Jacob stole away <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the heart of Laban.</ns0:note> unawares to Laban<ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Stole away the heart of</ns0:hi> Laban, to wit, his daughters, his cattle, and his gods, upon which his heart was vehe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mently set, as <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>s</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 18. 24. But if this had been meant, it had been imputed to <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> and not to <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> who knew nothing of the Gods. Or rather, <ns0:hi>stole away from the heart,</ns0:hi> &c. the Hebrew <ns0:hi>eth</ns0:hi> being put for <ns0:hi>meeth</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 1. and 49. 25. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 8. 43. compared with 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 6. 33. <ns0:hi>Mic.</ns0:hi> 3. 8. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> without the knowledge and consent of <ns0:hi>Laban,</ns0:hi> which sence is confirmed by the words next following, and by <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 26, 27. and by the like use of the phrase, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 3. Thus he fled because he knew <ns0:hi>Labans</ns0:hi> selfish and unrighteous and cruel disposition, that he would always hinder him from de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parting either by fraudulent pretences, or by open force, nor suffer so great a diminution in that estate, which he thought one time or other he might in good measure recover to himself.</ns0:note> the Syrian, in that he told him not that he fled.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 So he fled with all that he had, and he rose up and passed over the river <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Euphrates,</ns0:hi> which lay between <ns0:hi>Mesopotamia</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Chaldea, Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. 18. which for its largeness and famousness is oft called the <ns0:hi>River</ns0:hi> emphatically, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23. 31. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 24. 2, 3. &c.</ns0:note>, and set his face <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">

                     <ns0:hi>toward</ns0:hi> the mount Gilead <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">A very high and long mountain beyond <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> adjoyning to the Mountain of <ns0:hi>Lebanon,</ns0:hi> at the foot of which there was a large and fruitful country which from the Mountain received the name of <ns0:hi>Gilead, Deut.</ns0:hi> 34. 1. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 8. 22. and 22. 6. This Mountain is here called <ns0:hi>Gilead</ns0:hi> by anticipation, as appears from <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 48.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And it was told Laban on the third day <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">That he heard of it no sooner must be ascribed to the great distance which <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> had put between his and Jacobs flocks, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 36. and to the care and art which <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> used to prevent a sooner discovery.</ns0:note>, that Jacob was fled.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And he took his brethren with him; and pursued after him seven dayes journey, and they overtook him in the mount Gilead:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And God came to Laban the Syrian <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 33. 15.</ns0:note> in a dream by night, and said unto him, Take heed that thou speak not to Jacob <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from good to bad.</ns0:note> either good or bad <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Neither perswading him by flattering promises and cunning<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Artifices, nor compelling him by threatnings, to return. For so these general words must be limited, as is evident from Gods design in them, and from the following Relation. So this is a Synecdochical expression.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Then Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the Mount, and Laban with his brethren pitched in the mount of Gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And Laban said to Jacob, What hast thou done, that thou hast stollen away unawares to me, and carried away my daughters as captives <ns0:hi>taken</ns0:hi> with the sword <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">By force and violence.                   <ns0:p n="28">28 And hast not suffered me to kiss my sons and my daughters <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">As was usual at the parting of Friends. See the note on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 29. 11.</ns0:note>? thou hast now done foolish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly in so doing <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But indeed <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> took the wisest course for the security of his Person and Estate, especially having the direction and protection of God in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 It is in the power of my hand to do you hurt: but the God of your father <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> by which he disowns him for his God, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                  <ns0:p n="30">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:32" />30 And now <ns0:hi>though</ns0:hi> thou wouldst needs be gone, because thou sore longedst after thy fathers house, <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> wherefore hast thou stoln my Gods <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> could not be so senceless as to take those for true Gods which could be stollen away, but he calleth them <ns0:hi>Gods,</ns0:hi> because they were the means or representations whereby he worshipped his Gods.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="35">35 And she said to her father, Let it not dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />please my Lord, that I cannot rise up before thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How could that occasion hinder her from rising up to her Father? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. It might be attended in her, as it was and is in some other women, especially in those hot countries, with a greater flux of blood, or with more than ordinary infir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity and sickness; and this Laban might know to be usual with her by former observation or information. 2. She offers this as a reason not why she could not rise up to shew a civility to him, but why she could not <ns0:hi>rise up from his face,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>from before him,</ns0:hi> as the words in the Hebrew sound, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> so as to give way to him that he might come and search there for the Images: because menstruous women were antiently esteemed polluted and to pol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lute the things which they touched or sat upon, as you may see by <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 15. 19, 20, 21, 22. Which law though it were not yet given and written, yet that as well as divers other Ceremo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nial Rites might be enjoyned by God and observed by sober Heathens at that time, especially by such as were akin to <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />braham,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> and his Family were, who by that means might easily come to the knowledge of such matters. Add to this, one of the seven precepts given to the Sons of <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> was that of <ns0:hi>uncover<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing nakedness;</ns0:hi> which both Jewish and Christian writers take to be a very comprehensive expression and to include all such things as have a natural turpitude in them, among which this is confessed to be one. And the words thus understood contain a solid and satisfactory reason why <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> should not now come near her, nor search the things upon which she sat upon, which had been an uncivil and immodest thing.</ns0:note>; for the custom of women is upon me: and he searched, but found not the Images.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 And Jacob was very wroth, and chode with Laban, and Jacob answered, and said to Laban, What is my Trespass? what is my sin, that thou hast so hotly pursued after me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">With so much fury and violence.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 Whereas thou hast <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> felt.</ns0:note> searched all my stuff, what hast thou found of all thy houshold-stuff? set it here before my brethren, and thy brethren, that they may judge betwixt us both.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 This twenty years <ns0:hi>have</ns0:hi> I <ns0:hi>been</ns0:hi> with thee: thy ewes, and thy she-goats have not cast their young <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which thou owest in a great measure to my care and dili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gence in ordering them, and principally to Gods blessing given to thee for my sake, by thy own confession, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 27.</ns0:note>, and the rams of thy flock have I not eaten.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 That which was torn <ns0:hi>of beasts</ns0:hi> I brought not unto thee, I bare the loss of it: of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 22. 12.</ns0:note> my hand didst thou require it <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which was unjust and unreasonable, except where it fell out through the Shepherds default, See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 13. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> How could Jacob pay these losses, seeing he came empty from his Fathers house, and got nothing by his service for the first 14 years, but his wives? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Either 1. he had some sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plies sent from his Father, though it be not mentioned in this History: or 2. he might have some inconsiderable allowances or priviledges from <ns0:hi>Laban,</ns0:hi> out of which he could easily de<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ray these charges which because of his great care and watchfulness did but seldom happen: or 3. these losses were put to his ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count, to be satisfied by him as soon as he should be able to do it.</ns0:note>, whether stollen by day, or stollen by night.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40 <ns0:hi>Thus</ns0:hi> I was in the day, the drought consum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parted from mine eyes <ns0:note n="‖" place="bottom">Through my extraordinary thoughtfulness and care about thy cattle, especially in cases of danger.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 Thus have I been twenty years in thy house: I served thee fourteen years for thy two daughters, and six years for thy cattel; and thou hast chang<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed my wages ten times.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">42 Except the God of my Father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The God whom my father <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> worships with reve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence and godly fear, as appears by comparing <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 53. The act is here put for the Object, as it frequently is, and particular<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly God is called our <ns0:hi>fear, Isa.</ns0:hi> 8. 13. And <ns0:hi>fear</ns0:hi> is one of Gods names amongst the Rabbins. He calls him not <ns0:hi>Isaacs God,</ns0:hi> but his <ns0:hi>fear,</ns0:hi> because <ns0:hi>Isaac</ns0:hi> was yet alive and in the state of probation and served God with fear and trembling. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27. 33. The Jews observe, that God is not called the God of any par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular person, as of <ns0:hi>Abraham, Isaac</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> till after their death.</ns0:note> had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty: God hath seen my affliction <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">With compassion and intention of good to me for it. Gods <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> is oft used for his relieving and helping, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 16. 13. and 29. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>2. <ns0:hi>Exod</ns0:hi> 3. 7, 9. Or, <ns0:hi>hath shewed</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>proved</ns0:hi> it, to wit, that <ns0:hi>he hath seen,</ns0:hi> &c. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. Either way it is an Ellipsis of the pronoun, which is usual, as appears by comparing 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 10. 7. with 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. and <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 41. 9. with <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 13. 18.</ns0:note>, and the labour of mine hands, and rebuked <ns0:hi>thee</ns0:hi> yesternight.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 And Laban answered, and said unto Jacob, These daughters are my daughters, and these chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren are my children, and these cattel are my cat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tel, and all that thou <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eest is mine: and what can I do this day unto these my daughters, or unto their children which they have born <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He pretends that to be an act of his natural affection and kindness which was indeed the effect of his fear.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 Now therefore come thou, let us make a covenant, I and thou: and let it be for a witness between me and thee <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Both to our own consciences of our mutual Obligations, and to God against either of us who shall break it, that he may se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verely punish us for it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a pillar <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In Testimony of his compliance with Labans proposal and his entring into this Covenant. See <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 24. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="46">46 And Jacob said unto his brethren, Gather stones: and they took stones, and made an heap, and they did eat <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, afterwards, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 54. though it be here mentioned by anticipation.</ns0:note> there upon the heap <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or rather <ns0:hi>by</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>beside the heap,</ns0:hi> as the Hebrew particle <ns0:hi>al</ns0:hi> is oft understood, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 23. 2. and 81. 7.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="47">47 And Laban called it <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:hi>the heap of witness.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Jegar-sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Both names signifie the same thing, <ns0:hi>an heap of witness,</ns0:hi> onely <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> gives the name in the <ns0:hi>Syrian</ns0:hi> Language; but <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> though he had been long conversant in <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> and understood that Lan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guage, yet he chose to give it in <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> which was both a se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cret renouncing of the <ns0:hi>Syrian</ns0:hi> Manners and Religion together with their Language, and an implicit profession of his conjuncti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on with the <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> as in their Tongue so in their Religion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 And Laban said, This heap is a witness be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween me and thee this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="49">49 And <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:hi>abea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />con,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>watch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tower.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Mizpah: for he said, The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="50">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:32" />50 If thou shalt afflict my daughters, or if thou shalt take <ns0:hi>other</ns0:hi> wives beside my daughters <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The curse is here understood, as it commonly is, to main<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain a greater reverence for Oaths, and to beget a greater dread of the curse belonging to the violators of it.</ns0:note>, no <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> is with us <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Here <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> now <ns0:hi>no</ns0:hi> man <ns0:hi>with us,</ns0:hi> who, when we are parted, can witness and judge between us and punish the Transgressour. Or thus, Though now we have many with us, as witnesses of this agree<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, yet shortly when we shall be parted, <ns0:hi>no</ns0:hi> man will be <ns0:hi>with us,</ns0:hi> to observe and report our actions to the other, or to do the injur'd person right.</ns0:note>; See, God is witness betwixt me and thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 And Laban said to Jacob, Behold this heap, and behold this pillar, which I have cast betwixt me and thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="52">52 This heap be Witness, and this pillar be witness, that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap, and this pillar unto me, for harm.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="53">53 The God of Abraham, and the God of Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hor, the God of their father <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">He joyns Idols with the true God, and secretly chargeth the Religion of <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> with novelty, and prefers his own as the most antient Religion. See <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 24. 2. whence we may learn, that Antiquity of it self is no certain argument of the true Church or Religion.</ns0:note>, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="54">54 Then Jacob <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> killed beasts.</ns0:note> offered sacrifice <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Either to give God thanks for the great mercies and deli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />verances vouchsased to him, or to beg Gods blessing upon the present treaty and upon their whole family. But it is not so probable that <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi> would chuse that time for the offering of Sacrifices when <ns0:hi>Laban</ns0:hi> was present, whom he could neither ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nestly admit to them, nor conveniently exclude from them. And therefore seeing the same Hebrew word signifies <ns0:hi>killing</ns0:hi> as well as <ns0:hi>sacrificing,</ns0:hi> as appears from <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 22. 40. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 28. 24. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 1. 9. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 18. 2. &c. I rather understand it of his <ns0:hi>killing of beasts</ns0:hi> in order to a Feast, which he made for his brethren, whom <ns0:hi>he called,</ns0:hi> as it here follows, <ns0:hi>to eat bread,</ns0:hi> &c. under which phrase all meats are usually comprehended in Scripture, as hath been already noted, and will appear here<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />after. And this practise was usual in those times to confirm Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venants by a Feast. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 26. 30.</ns0:note> upon the mount, and called his brethren to eat bread, and they did eat bread, and tarried all night in the mount.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="55">55 And early in the morning, Laban rose up and kissed his sons, and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place.</ns0:p>
